narrative.note: Riley is four, and every subject on this report is just getting started, which is exactly where four is supposed to be, Jordan. The one thing most worth your time this month is sound play. Try clapping out the beats in words like ba-na-na, or playing sound I-spy in the car: it's the foundation reading is built on.

subjects.math: Counting objects one at a time and landing on a total is next for Riley. Touching each stair or cracker while counting turns that practice into a game.
subjects.literacy: Riley hasn't yet started asking what a sign or cereal box says, and a daily letter hunt is a playful way to spark that curiosity.
subjects.phonics: Clapping out the beats in a word, like ba-na-na, is the next sound skill for Riley. Sound I-spy turns listening into a game you can play anywhere.
subjects.writing: Riley is still working toward holding a crayon with fingers instead of a fist. Writing a big name in marker for Riley to trace gives that grip lots of practice.
subjects.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier today is next for Riley. Handing over the story after something fun builds that retelling muscle.
subjects.science: Sorting things into groups, like big versus small or animals versus plants, is next for Riley. Sink or float turns the guessing before each item drops into the game itself.
subjects.social_studies: Naming family members and how they connect is next for Riley. Drawing a map of home together, with a star for each person's bed, makes that first map fun.
subjects.art: Naming main colors while drawing or painting is next for Riley. Drawing how a song feels, fast scribbles for fast parts, gives color naming a reason to happen.
subjects.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat is next for Riley. Copy my clap, swapping leaders, turns that rhythm practice into play.
subjects.gross_motor: Galloping, with one foot leading the other, is next for Riley. Animal races down the hallway, bear crawl, crab walk, frog jump, build that coordination.
subjects.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces is next for Riley. Snipping paper into confetti with child-safe scissors builds that same hand control.
subjects.social_emotional: Playing WITH other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders, is next for Riley. Naming a feeling before offering two choices helps that turn-taking grow.
subjects.self_care: Using the toilet during the day, with only the occasional miss, is next for Riley. A button board turns practice into a game instead of a morning rush.
subjects.executive_function: Waiting a short turn without falling apart, even with support, is next for Riley. Freeze dance turns that waiting practice into a dance party.
subjects.computer_science: Playing 'robot,' giving and following exact steps, is a fun way to explore coding whenever it fits into your days with Riley. There's no age clock on this one, just whatever pace feels fun.
subjects.spanish: Understanding everyday words in another language, like water or milk, is something Riley can pick up whenever you like. Picking one phrase to use all week is a simple way to start.

narrative.synthesis: Riley's literacy and phonics lines both point toward reading: noticing that words carry meaning and hearing the sounds inside them are the two skills that build toward it. Since reading is what you asked about, sound play is worth leaning into this month. A few minutes of sound I-spy or clapping out word beats during everyday moments, like the car or bath time, builds that ear without any pressure to rush toward letters yet.

drawers.math: One-to-one counting is the base every later math skill builds on, so this is exactly the right place to start. Once Riley can count and land on a total, comparing and adding will follow naturally.
drawers.literacy: Curiosity about what words say usually shows up before actual reading does, so this is an early and encouraging thing to watch for. It tends to follow once letter awareness starts to build.
drawers.phonics: Hearing the separate beats in a word is one of the strongest early markers for reading, since reading is really sounds mapped onto letters. Building that ear now sets up everything that follows.
drawers.writing: Grip develops before letter formation does, so strengthening those finger muscles now sets up smoother writing later. There's no rush toward letters until the grip feels comfortable.
drawers.language: Retelling a recent event takes both memory and sequencing, two skills that grow together around this age. Giving Riley the floor to narrate, rather than asking yes or no questions, is what invites that skill out.
drawers.science: Sorting is the first form of scientific thinking Riley will use, well before any formal science ideas arrive. Naming categories out loud during everyday moments is what turns noticing into sorting.
drawers.social_studies: Understanding how family members connect is Riley's earliest sense of social structure. A visual map gives that abstract idea something concrete to point to.
drawers.art: Naming colors while creating links language and observation in a way plain looking doesn't. It's less about art skill and more about vocabulary catching up to what Riley already sees.
drawers.music: Keeping a steady beat is a physical skill before it becomes a musical one, tied to the same timing sense used in movement. Practicing it playfully now is enough.
drawers.gross_motor: Galloping asks one side of the body to lead while the other follows, a coordination step past the simpler running and jumping Riley already has. It tends to click with repetition rather than instruction.
drawers.fine_motor: Threading and stringing ask for the same pincer control that holding a pencil will need later. Scissors work builds that same hand strength in a way that feels like play.
drawers.social_emotional: Playing WITH others, not just alongside them, is a real leap in social skill, and reminders are expected at this age. Practice with turn-taking in small doses builds the patience for longer play.
drawers.self_care: Daytime toileting is a body-readiness skill as much as a habit, and every child reaches it on their own schedule. Turning the related routines into a game takes the pressure off for everyone.
drawers.executive_function: Waiting through a short delay is one of the first forms of self-control Riley will practice, and support is expected at this age. Freeze dance gives that waiting a fun, low-stakes rehearsal.
drawers.computer_science: This one is entirely about exposure, not a timeline, so there's no pace to keep. Playing 'robot' introduces the idea of exact instructions long before any actual coding does.
drawers.spanish: Like coding, this is about exposure and comes from whatever the family chooses to do, never a schedule. Picking one phrase and using it all week is a small, sustainable way to start.

narrative.keepsake: Trucks are your world right now, Riley, wheels and engines and all the ways things move. Jordan gets to watch you dig into whatever catches your attention, fully and without holding back. Jordan loves the questions you ask and the way you notice small details other people might miss. Keep exploring at your own pace, Riley. There is so much ahead for you to discover. Homa
